black-sheet:
## What this is

The calibration sheet for the Breach triptych's paper stack. Three tabloid sheets (279.4 x 431.8 mm) are plotted, knife-cut, trimmed at the crop marks, stacked flat and glued: black paper at the bottom, gold-yellow paper over it, white paper on top. The white sheet has big windows (W1 upper left, W2 upper right) that show the gold sheet, and the gold sheet has a window (G1, inside W2) that shows the black sheet. This sheet is only a test: it is not signed, and none of it is art.

It measures, before the real triptych is drawn:

- the real line width of each ink on each paper, and which inks read on which paper;
- how legible the cut guides are;
- how close art can sit to a knife cut (the margin);
- how far lower art must run under an upper edge (the bleed);
- how far apart the sheets register after trimming at the crop marks, read to 0.1 mm with verniers;
- whether art on a lower sheet ghosts through the paper above it.

## This sheet: black paper (the bottom ply)

Plot on black paper with twelve gel pens: the two Signo broads (gold and silver) and ten Moonlight 10s (fl pink, fl orange, green, fl yellow, fl vermilion, red, rose, purple, blue and teal). The red, rose, purple, blue and teal are on trial on black. The silver also inks the crop marks. It has no cuts: trim it at the crop marks and it is done. Window G1 shows the swatches of the triptych's six pens (Signo gold and silver, Moonlight fl pink, fl orange, green and fl yellow), the bleed ladder and the x and y main scales for the gold-over-black verniers once the gold sheet is on top. The silver hatch box in the lower left is the ghost test hidden under the gold and white papers. Everything else lies outside G1 and is hidden once the stack is glued, so read it on the loose sheet: the spacing ladder (upper left), the ink crossings below it, dots and dashes below the ghost box, the font test (right, below G1), the swatches of the other six pens below the font test, and an edge ruler at the middle of each side.

## Pens, in plot order

The dashboard asks for each layer by its id. Every test on the sheet is labelled, in its own ink, with the name of the pen that should have drawn it: a label in the wrong colour means the wrong pen was fitted for that layer.

1. `silver`: Signo broad silver
2. `fluoro-pink`: Moonlight 10 fl pink
3. `fluoro-orange`: Moonlight 10 fl orange
4. `gold`: Signo broad gold
5. `fluoro-green`: Moonlight 10 green
6. `fluoro-yellow`: Moonlight 10 fl yellow
7. `fluoro-vermilion`: Moonlight 10 fl vermilion
8. `gel-red`: Moonlight 10 red
9. `gel-rose`: Moonlight 10 rose
10. `gel-purple`: Moonlight 10 purple
11. `gel-blue`: Moonlight 10 blue
12. `gel-teal`: Moonlight 10 teal
13. `finishing-border`: Signo broad silver (the crop marks)

## Plot, cut and assemble

1. Plot all three sheets (black, gold and white) on their own paper, one pen layer after another in the order of the pen plan, without moving the paper. Gel inks marked "(trial)" are being tried on that paper for the first time.
2. Let the gel ink dry at least 1 hour before cutting.
3. Cut each sheet's windows along the **outer edge** of the drawn outline (the knife goes on the line the outline just touches). Black sheet: no windows. Gold sheet: G1, and the cut ladder in its lower left. White sheet: W1, W2 and the five small windows A, B, C, D and E (E is the margin-ladder window).
4. Trim every sheet at its crop marks.
5. Stack flat, bottom to top: black, gold, white, squared in an L-square against the same corner, then glue.

## What to read

- **Ink swatches** (each ink on its own paper): a 22 x 12 mm hatch patch at 0.6 mm pitch; beside it a single line, a dashed line and a 3 mm hatch strip at 0.3 mm pitch. Where the strip fuses to solid the line is wider than 0.3 mm. For each ink on each paper say whether it **reads**, is **weak** or **does not read**, and the single line's width if you can measure it.
- **Cut-guide variants** (white sheet, windows A to D, plotted before cutting): the X marks and label differ in pitch and size (A pitch 12, size 4; B pitch 8, size 3; C pitch 16, size 6; D no label). Say which is the **smallest variant that is still obvious** to cut by.
- **Margin ladder** (white sheet beside window E, gold sheet above window G1): four lines at 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 mm from the cut line. After cutting, find the line closest to the cut that the knife **spared** (whole, not nicked or cut away). That offset is the working margin.
- **Bleed ladder** (gold sheet at the bottom edge of W1, black sheet at the bottom edge of G1): seven lines that end -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 mm past the edge (negative: they stop short, inside the window). After assembly, find the **shortest line that shows no gap** at the edge. That offset is the working bleed.
- **Ghosts** (white sheet, the two boxes captioned "is there a ghost here?"): the left box lies over a dense silver hatch on the black sheet, under both the gold and white papers; the right box lies over a dense black hatch on the gold sheet, under the white paper. Say whether either hatch shows through.
- **Font test** (each sheet, each of its inks): the word "line" in the Hershey sans face and then in the script face, at 1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 and 5 mm (cap height), left to right on one baseline, and below them "everything falls into line" in sans at 2.6 mm, the size the triptych's phrase is drawn at (on the art each word rides one of the lines, in that line's ink). For each ink on each paper find the **smallest size that is still legible** at arm's length, in sans and in script, and say whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads. The black sheet's font test is hidden once the sheets are glued: read it before gluing.
- **Spacing ladder** (each sheet, each pen; white: Micron 01 black, Micron 05 blue and Moonlight 10 fl pink): 5 x 5 mm hatch patches at 0.40, 0.50, 0.55, 0.66, 0.80 and 1.00 mm between line centres, then a 3 mm square outlined twice and three times at 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 mm. Find the **tightest spacing whose lines stay separate** (not fused to solid), for hatch, doubles and triples.
- **Dots, dashes and tight curves** (each sheet, each ink as above): dash rows 0.3, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.6 mm on with gaps as long; a row of dots, three each of strokes 0.3, 0.35 and 0.4 mm long; crosses 0.8, 1.2 and 1.6 mm across (the sizes of the stars); circles of radius 0.5, 1, 2 and 4 mm; a spiral from 2 to 8 mm across. Find the **shortest dash** and the **smallest circle** that draw cleanly without skipping, and say whether the dots show. Two things the pipeline does, so they are expected: the 0.3 mm dashes come out as one line (finalize joins strokes whose ends are under 0.4 mm apart before the plotter gets them), and a true point never reaches the plotter (the render drops zero-length strokes and finalize any shorter than 0.3 mm), so the dots are the shortest strokes that do.
- **Ink crossings** (black sheet: all twelve pens; white: carbon, ultramarine, fluoro pink): every pair of inks crosses twice, the row's ink across and the column's ink down. The pen plotted later is on top, in the black's plot order (see Pens) and on the white Micron 01 black, Micron 05 blue, then Moonlight 10 fl pink. Say whether any crossing **smears or drags** the earlier ink, and if you plot a sheet a second time with a pause between pens (10 minutes or so), whether waiting helps.
- **Cut ladder** (gold sheet, lower left; cut it with G1, before gluing): wedges whose tips close to 60, 45, 30 and 20 degrees; slots 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm wide and 30 long; three windows round a kept island held by one bridge 2, 3 or 4 mm wide (as the shirt cut holds the tie at its knot and tip); a notch open to the bottom trim. Find the **sharpest wedge** whose tip cuts clean, the **narrowest slot** that cuts clean, the **narrowest bridge** that holds its island, and whether the notch cuts clean at the trim.
- **Edge rulers** (each sheet, the middle of each side): four short lines 12, 13, 14 and 16 mm from the paper edge, labelled, that is 1, 2, 3 and 5 mm inside the crop line (all art is clipped to the crop line, so the margin itself cannot carry lines). Before trimming, measure with a rule from the paper edge to the 12 line on each side: the difference from 12 mm is how far the plot landed from where it was placed on the bed.
- **Verniers** (read to 0.1 mm, with a loupe): there are four, two per neighbouring pair of sheets. White over gold at W1 and gold over black at G1 each have an **x** vernier on the window's bottom edge (it reads left-right registration) and a **y** vernier on its right edge (it reads up-down registration). Each has a main scale of 21 ticks at 1.00 mm on the lower sheet (10 mm either side of its 0 tick, every fifth tick longer, running 4 mm under the upper paper) and a vernier of 11 ticks at 0.90 mm on the upper sheet's paper, starting at the edge. The two 0 ticks line up when registration is perfect.
  - Find the vernier tick that continues in a straight line across the cut into a main-scale tick. Call its number k: 0 is the vernier's first tick, 10 its last, ticks 5 and 10 are longer.
  - The main-scale tick at or just before the vernier's 0 tick, counted from the main 0 tick, gives the whole millimetres, n. The vernier tick k that lines up gives the tenths.
  - Reading = n + 0.1 x k mm. The arrow marked + is the positive direction: positive means the upper sheet sits further right (x) or further down (y) than the lower one. Example: the vernier's 0 tick falls just past the main 0 tick and its tick 3 lines up: +0.3 mm. If the vernier's 0 tick falls just before the main 0 tick, n is -1: with tick 7 lined up the reading is -1 + 0.7 = -0.3 mm. The tenths can be read for shifts from about -10 mm to +2 mm; beyond that, report just the whole millimetres.

## Report back

- Line width per ink per paper: reads / weak / no (and the width of the single line if you can measure it).
- The smallest cut-guide variant (A, B, C or D) that is still obvious.
- The margin line the knife spared (0.5, 1.0, 1.5 or 2.0 mm), on the white and on the gold sheet.
- The gap-free bleed line (its label in mm), on the gold ladder (through W1) and the black one (through G1).
- The x and y vernier readings for each pair: white over gold (at W1) and gold over black (at G1). Note whether you read them before or after gluing.
- Whether any ghost shows (left box, right box).
- Font test: the smallest legible size per ink per paper, sans and script (1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5 or 5 mm), and whether the 2.6 mm phrase reads in each ink (above all Moonlight 10 fl pink on white, Signo gold on black and the Micron blacks on gold-yellow: the inks the phrase is drawn in).
- Spacing ladder: the tightest separate spacing per ink per paper, for hatch, doubles and triples.
- Dots, dashes and curves: the shortest clean dash and the smallest clean circle per ink per paper, and whether the dots show.
- Crossings: any smear or drag (which pair, which way), and whether a pause between pens helps.
- Cut ladder: the sharpest clean wedge, the narrowest clean slot, the narrowest bridge that held, and the notch.
- Edge rulers: the measured distance from the paper edge to the 12 mm line on each side (top, bottom, left, right), per sheet.

Nothing is plotted or cut until you say go.

- **Ink crossings** (black sheet: all twelve pens; white: carbon, ultramarine, fluoro pink): every pair of inks crosses twice, the row's ink across and the column's ink down. The pen plotted later is on top, in the black's plot order (see Pens) and on the white Micron 01 black, Micron 05 blue, then Moonlight 10 fl pink. Say whether any crossing **smears or drags** the earlier ink, and if you plot a sheet a second time with a pause between pens (10 minutes or so), whether waiting helps.
- **Cut ladder** (gold sheet, lower left; cut it with G1, before gluing): wedges whose tips close to 60, 45, 30 and 20 degrees; slots 3, 4, 5 and 6 mm wide and 30 long; three windows round a kept island held by one bridge 2, 3 or 4 mm wide (as the shirt cut holds the tie at its knot and tip); a notch open to the bottom trim. Find the **sharpest wedge** whose tip cuts clean, the **narrowest slot** that cuts clean, the **narrowest bridge** that holds its island, and whether the notch cuts clean at the trim.
- **Edge rulers** (each sheet, the middle of each side): four short lines 12, 13, 14 and 16 mm from the paper edge, labelled, that is 1, 2, 3 and 5 mm inside the crop line (all art is clipped to the crop line, so the margin itself cannot carry lines). Before trimming, measure with a rule from the paper edge to the 12 line on each side: the difference from 12 mm is how far the plot landed from where it was placed on the bed.
- **Verniers** (read to 0.1 mm, with a loupe): there are four, two per neighbouring pair of sheets. White over gold at W1 and gold over black at G1 each have an **x** vernier on the window's bottom edge (it reads left-right registration) and a **y** vernier on its right edge (it reads up-down registration). Each has a main scale of 21 ticks at 1.00 mm on the lower sheet (10 mm either side of its 0 tick, every fifth tick longer, running 4 mm under the upper paper) and a vernier of 11 ticks at 0.90 mm on the upper sheet's paper, starting at the edge. The two 0 ticks line up when registration is perfect.
  - Find the vernier tick that continues in a straight line across the cut into a main-scale tick. Call its number k: 0 is the vernier's first tick, 10 its last, ticks 5 and 10 are longer.
  - The main-scale tick at or just before the vernier's 0 tick, counted from the main 0 tick, gives the whole millimetres, n. The vernier tick k that lines up gives the tenths.
  - Reading = n + 0.1 x k mm. The arrow marked + is the positive direction: positive means the upper sheet sits further right (x) or further down (y) than the lower one. Example: the vernier's 0 tick falls just past the main 0 tick and its tick 3 lines up: +0.3 mm. If the vernier's 0 tick falls just before the main 0 tick, n is -1: with tick 7 lined up the reading is -1 + 0.7 = -0.3 mm. The tenths can be read for shifts from about -10 mm to +2 mm; beyond that, report just the whole millimetres.
